title: Nimbus Analytics - GPU reservation & burst strategy kickoff
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-07-10 15:00 UTC | Duration: 42m | Recording: Fireflies.ai
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Owen Park (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Nimbus Head of ML), Sofia Lopez (Nimbus Infra), Ethan Kim (Nimbus CTO)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be partial): Discussed Dedicated capacity needs: reserved GPU sizing, isolation/VPC constraints, burst policy (elastic burst vs queued), autoscale windows, SLAs and security controls (KMS, SOC2), and next steps to share benchmarks and pricing.

00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and we can kick off — is this still good time zone wise?
00:06 Ravi Patel: Yep, all good from my side. Thanks Maya.
00:08 Ethan Kim: Morning for us, afternoon for you I guess, thanks.
00:12 Maya Chen: Cool. I'm Maya, AE for Redwood Inference, and with me is Owen Park our SE. Owen do you want to intro real quick?
00:20 Owen Park: Yeah hi folks, Owen Park, systems and inference performance. I work on dedicated sizing and kernel/quantization recommendations. Happy to go deep.
00:28 Sofia Lopez: Great. Quick context: Nimbus is moving from hosted endpoints on another vendor to either Redwood Hosted or a Dedicated pool. Main drivers are predictable latency for real-time features and data isolation for customer PII.
00:40 Maya Chen: Perfect, that's what we're here for. Can we go through current traffic profile and the constraints?
00:46 Ravi Patel: Sure. High level: models are a mix — local fine-tuned 3B variants and a few 13B open weights for higher quality. Real-time chat use-case: 90th percentile target 300 to 400ms token latency end-to-end. Peak QPS is spiky — our busiest minute can be 350 concurrent sessions generating short replies, average sequence length about 60 tokens. We also have nightly batch jobs for embeddings.
01:12 Owen Park: When you say 350 concurrent sessions do you mean in-flight token streams or separate requests per second?
01:17 Ravi Patel: In-flight, so streams. Each session roughly 2-3 tokens/sec on average, sometimes bursty when users paste text.
01:25 Owen Park: Got it. That helps with batching calculus. And what's your tolerance for degraded quality if we fall back to a quantized variant or smaller model under pressure?
01:35 Ethan Kim: We want graceful degradation. Prefer smaller model fallback over errors, but need to measure throughput/latency tradeoff. Also need audit logs and key management for any private deployment.
01:45 Maya Chen: Totally. Two typical Redwood options: Hosted with autoscaling (fast to start) or Dedicated reserved GPU pool (predictable throughput + VPC isolation). Dedicated supports burst capacity — configurable bursts to handle short spikes, or you can design a queued burst with early rejections.
02:03 Sofia Lopez: On isolation: we need VPC peering, customer-managed KMS, and support for our private subnets. We also need to know whether GPUs are tenant-isolated (single-tenant) or multi-tenant on the node.
02:15 Owen Park: For Dedicated we can do customer-dedicated instances (single-tenant) — that's our Dedicated Dedicated mode, sorry the naming is confusing — or shared-hosted instances in a reserved pool. Single-tenant means full isolation physically at GPU level; shared-reserved means the pool is reserved for you but other tenants could pack if you allow.
02:35 Ravi Patel: What's the tradeoff? Cost vs utilization, right?
02:38 Owen Park: Exactly. Single-tenant ups cost but gives you strict tenancy, helpful for compliance. Shared-reserved is cheaper and still gives consistent capacity but we may colocate low-priority workloads if you enable bursting to other zones.
02:50 Ethan Kim: You mentioned burst policy earlier — can you elaborate on how Redwood handles bursts?
02:55 Maya Chen: There are a few levers: short-term burst credits (we preconfigure headroom for X minutes), autoscale with warm pools (pre-warmed containers/VMs to reduce cold starts), and cross-region fallback. For Dedicated customers we usually recommend a small baseline of reserved GPUs sized for 95th percentile, plus burst headroom for the 99th minute.
03:13 Owen Park: One more option is throttled queuing with adaptive batching: we accept requests into a short queue (50-200ms) to improve batch formation. That lets you serve higher effective throughput without provisioning as many GPUs but increases tail latency slightly.
03:28 Sofia Lopez: Hmm, we care a lot about tail latency. 50-200ms queue might push us over our SLA at 95th. What are real numbers you've seen for similar profiles?
03:36 Owen Park: For a 13B model on A100-like GPUs, with optimized kernels and continuous batching, we've seen 95th token latency between 120-300ms depending on sequence length and batch size. The queue adds the batching delay (e.g., 40-120ms), but improves cost.
03:52 Ravi Patel: Any quantization impact? We are open to int8 if quality is within tolerance.
03:56 Owen Park: int8 usually reduces memory and improves throughput significantly. Quality delta is model dependent; we can run evals on your prompt set. We recommend running a small pilot with both int8 and fp16 variants and compare.
04:06 Maya Chen: I'll note action on the pilot. Owen, also mention KV cache/long sequences — Nimbus has some long context cases, correct?
04:13 Ravi Patel: Right, we have occasional 4k contexts for conversation history, but most are 512. So memory profile swings.
04:20 Owen Park: That matters for kernel selection. We can do per-route model variants: short-context route pinned to quantized small models and long-context route to larger pinned instances. Routing is supported in the platform.
04:31 Sofia Lopez: About security and auditing — we need daily audit logs, SSO via SAML, and vendor certs (SOC2 Type II). Can Redwood host keys in our KMS or do we have to use Redwood-managed keys?
04:44 Maya Chen: For Dedicated Private deployments we support customer KMS/HSM integrations and SAML SSO + RBAC. Hosted can use customer-managed KMS in Private plans; we'll send the options in the security pack.
04:55 Ethan Kim: Good. We will need the SOC2 docs and a network diagram for our security review.
04:59 Maya Chen: Yes, we'll attach those.
05:02 Ravi Patel: Ok practical question: what's the typical lead time for reserved GPU capacity and for private deployment with VPC peering?
05:09 Owen Park: Reserved capacity for standard pool sizing is usually 2-4 weeks depending on region and GPU type. Private VPC deployments typically 4-8 weeks — there are network approvals and provisioning. If you need faster, we sometimes do temporary hosted with IP allowlist while the dedicated setup completes.
05:24 Maya Chen: Also note our Dedicated SLA and uptime targets differ by contract/tier. We'll surface the standard SLO doc in the follow-up.
05:30 Sofia Lopez: Pricing — we need both commitment (monthly/annual) and overage/burst pricing so we can model TCO.
05:36 Maya Chen: We'll include a couple of commitment tiers and a burst pricing table. For burst we usually offer a short headroom (metered at a premium) or a priority queue where requests may be preempted.
05:48 Ravi Patel: For capacity planning we have two modes internally: strict isolation for enterprise customers (single-tenant) and pooled for self-service. Likely we'll want single-tenant for enterprise customers but pooled for public-facing features. Can Redwood support hybrid?
05:59 Owen Park: Yes, we support hybrid routing. You can pin enterprise tenant traffic to single-tenant GPUs and route public routes to the reserved pooled nodes. That also enables different rollback/rollout strategies per route.
06:14 Ethan Kim: How do you handle model rollouts/versions in Dedicated? Can we do canary traffic splits?
06:19 Maya Chen: Yes, per-route rollout policies, canary traffic, A/B experiments, and automatic fallback to a pinned older model if regression detected. We also integrate with evals so you can automate quality checks.
06:30 Ravi Patel: For benchmarking, what do you need from us to give a tight sizing recommendation?
06:34 Owen Park: Ideal: 48-hour traffic traces (per-request timestamps, seq len, tokens generated), a few representative prompts+ground-truths for quality eval, and the model weights or exact model names + any fine-tunes. Also your acceptable latency targets and cost constraints.
06:49 Ravi Patel: We can share traffic traces and sample prompts. We may not share model weights yet — they're internal — but we can provide the exact base model and tuning details.
06:58 Maya Chen: That's fine. We'll run internal benchmark harness with the same models. But if you can do a short pilot with sample requests on a Dedicated trial we can get real numbers.
07:07 Sofia Lopez: Trial — what's included in a trial? Do we get pre-warmed GPUs and burst headroom?
07:12 Owen Park: Trials vary. Typically we provision limited reserved capacity for 2-4 weeks with baseline throughput and limited burst credits. It's not unlimited but it's real capacity so you can validate latency and routing.
07:25 Ethan Kim: Anything about failure modes — if a node goes down during peak, what's the observed failover and how much degraded performance?
07:33 Owen Park: We replicate model artifacts and maintain warm spare capacity in the pool. Failover depends on how much headroom you reserve. If you're at 100% utilization, failover can cause tail latency spikes and queued requests; if you've got 10-20% spare, the platform can absorb one node failure with minimal impact.
07:50 Ravi Patel: So recommended capacity planning rule of thumb? 95th baseline + 10-20% buffer + burst credits for minute-level spikes?
07:58 Maya Chen: That's a common rule. We can model it for your trace and propose a few commit tiers: conservative (95th + 20%), cost-optimized (95th baseline + small buffer + more aggressive batching), and enterprise isolated (single-tenant, higher cost).
08:15 Sofia Lopez: Can Redwood provide per-route cost attribution? We want to know which product lines are driving tokens.
08:20 Maya Chen: Yes, console shows token-level cost breakdown per API key/route with traces to model versions. That data can be exported for internal chargeback.
08:28 Ravi Patel: Ok let's talk timeline. We're aiming to make a vendor decision in 6 weeks to start pilots in 8 weeks. Any blockers?
08:35 Maya Chen: That timeline aligns. We'll need your traffic traces and decisions on single-tenant vs pooled for the initial scope. Also security review may add time.
08:42 Ethan Kim: We'll route security review to our InfoSec during this window.
08:45 Sofia Lopez: Any integration work for our infra — like peering, route tables, egress, IP allowlist?
08:51 Owen Park: We'll share a network checklist. For private deployments we need BGP/peering details, allowed CIDR ranges, and service account provisioning. For hosted reserved pools we often do IP allowlist + SAML.
08:59 Maya Chen: Quick demo ask: do you want Owen to run a mini benchmark next week with your sample prompts against a hostded quantized variant and a dedicated fp16 variant?
09:08 Ravi Patel: Yes please, that would be great. Prefer the 13B model results, and a 3B variant for baseline.
09:15 Maya Chen: Great. Let's capture action items.

Summary (human-typed recap):
- Need: predictable latency for real-time features, data isolation for PII, hybrid tenancy (single-tenant for enterprise, pooled for public).
- Traffic: spiky in-flight streams, peak minute ~350 sessions, mostly short sequences but occasional 4k contexts.
- Options discussed: Dedicated single-tenant vs reserved pool, burst credits, pre-warm, queued batching, fallback to quantized variants.
- Security: SAML SSO, KMS/HSM integration supported, SOC2 docs requested.
- Timeline: decision in ~6 weeks, pilots in ~8 weeks.

Action items and next steps (below)

10:00 Action items (as captured in call):
- Maya Chen: Send Dedicated pricing tiers + burst pricing table + standard SLO doc and SOC2 link by 2025-07-12.
- Owen Park: Run bench on 13B fp16 vs int8 and 3B baseline using provided sample prompts; deliver results and spreadsheet by 2025-07-16.
- Ravi Patel: Share 48-hour traffic traces and representative prompt set by 2025-07-15. (will anonymize PII)
- Sofia Lopez: Confirm VPC peering constraints and whether single-tenant nodes required; send network contact info by 2025-07-14.
- Ethan Kim: Schedule InfoSec review touchpoint; propose times for next week.

Transcription notes: medium quality; some technical terms may be slightly mistranscribed (e.g., KV cache as K V cache).

End of transcript.
